en: Regarding the statement, "The śramaṇa Zhizhou composed a commentary;
Vasubandhu immediately understood it," etc.: according to the second fascicle of that treatise, it says, "All seeds further have six meanings.
As for 'momentary extinction' (kṣaṇika-nirodha), it means that both types of seeds are necessarily uninterrupted."
Because it perishes and disintegrates. Why is this?
A permanent dharma cannot serve as the essence of a seed.
"Because at all times its nature is as it was originally, without distinction. The commentary states:
"The two types of seeds refer to internal and external seeds. 'Simultaneously existing' means..."
That is to say, neither the past nor the future, nor that which is dissociated, can serve as a seed.
Why? Because if the seed were to exist at this time [in those states],...
Because the fruit arises at that very moment, it "continually evolves" (nitya-anuvartaka).
This refers to the ālayavijñāna continuing until its antidote arises,
and external factors continuing until their seeds persist and the faculties remain.
Or even until it is matured. Regarding the term "definitive" (*niyata*):
it means that these seeds are individually determined;
they do not arise from everything out of everything.
Regarding "from this seed, that very thing arises again, depending upon various conditions":
this means that this seed must depend upon its own specific collection of conditions in order to produce a fruit;
it cannot produce everything at all times.
If, at this place and at this time, it encounters its own specific conditions,
then at this very place and at this very time, its own fruit arises. That which can only produce its own fruit refers to its own seed, which produces only its own fruit.
Just as the seeds of the ālayavijñāna can only produce the ālayavijñāna,
and just as rice grains and the like can only produce fruits such as rice, other [types of] seeds are not mentioned here regarding external phenomena.
Because it is easy, it is not discussed;
rather, the difficult is cited to illuminate [the easy].
At the beginning of the text, it is stated that [the Buddha knows] "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*).
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "also clarifying for the great assembly," there are briefly two explanations.
The first states that the twelve links of dependent origination are not [the meaning of] "this."
It is not a seed. Regarding the statement "unconditioned, without grasping, and so forth," this explains the reason why.
Second, the phrase "it is not" belongs to the subsequent clause.
This reveals that the essence of dependent origination is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The statement "without grasping," etc., explains the reason for this.
The preceding explanation serves as the basis.
This is intended to clarify that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a seed;
it is not for the purpose of refuting the meaning of the unconditioned itself. Question: From this discussion, another question arises.
If the opponent were to offer a defense, saying: "Although the essential nature of the unconditioned is not produced by conditions..."
And yet, one is able to establish the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) by setting it apart from those [other categories].
What fault is there in this?
It is just like the meanings of perception (saṃjñā), feeling (vedanā), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). One should answer and challenge them as follows:
Furthermore, does this unconditioned possess functional efficacy or not?
If it possesses functional efficacy, it should not be unconditioned.
Because it possesses functional capacity, it is like the phenomena that are separated by it;
if it lacked functional capacity, how could it effect separation? If this is so, then in the Mahāyāna, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are likewise so:
all noble ones (*ārya*) are differentiated precisely by means of the unconditioned.
The two faults are likewise the same. Answer: There is only a distinction based on the varying degrees of depth in the realization of the noble ones (*ārya*).
How could there be any functional capacity within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that causes such distinctions among the noble ones?
Therefore, they cannot be treated as analogous cases.
If one were to claim that the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is itself dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*),
the fault would be even more severe.

This can be understood through reflection. There is a doctrine that also refutes the Sthavira position that a single momentary mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) possess a sequence of arising first and ceasing later;
rather, it holds that material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) undergo the four phases of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
Regarding the sequence of the three—abiding, change, and cessation—occurring in the present single moment according to the ancient Sarvāstivādins:
in detail, it is said that this principle is not necessarily so.
For although they maintain that these two, four, or three dharmas exist simultaneously, [the logic remains problematic].
All are said to perish in a single thought-moment, which is called "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇa-nirodha*).
If you object that this is not accepted because a single thought-moment contains multiple dharmas occurring together,
[we reply that] when a seed produces a sprout, three dharmas occur simultaneously.
The seed should not be the seed.
If it is argued that it is not the seed because that [opponent] maintains there is a sequence,
this might exclude the Sthavira.
According to our school, how could a single moment be divided into temporal parts?
Why, then, would one exclude it?
The text of the treatise merely negates the existence of a permanent, unchanging dharma.
How could those two, four, and three not occasionally undergo transformation?
For this reason, it does not necessarily exclude their arising and so forth.
Nevertheless, the principle of the incidental exclusion [of other meanings] should also apply here.
The Commentary states:
"This clarifies the distinction from that seventh [consciousness].
This means that when a person of no-nature (*abhāva*) manifests the seventh consciousness and perfumes seeds, although it is simultaneously present with its fruit, [it is excluded].
Because the essential nature of the seed-fruit is submerged and hidden, the seven [consciousnesses] that manifest are not called "seeds.

Question: The treatise states, "That is to say, [they are seeds] because they give rise to manifest fruit-dharmas," thereby distinguishing them from the various manifest consciousnesses which are not called seeds. What does this mean?
Question: What is the purpose of adding the character "manifest" (xiàn) at the end of the treatise?

Why trouble the commentary with the explanation that it serves to distinguish [the seed] from what is merely manifest? Answer: If the character "manifest" were not present at the end, there would be the doubt that causes which lack a substantial entity, as well as those existing in the past or future, could also be designated as "seeds."
The term "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) is established in order to exclude this [possibility]. If that is so, then within the category of the manifest, only two meanings are subsumed;

since the preceding term "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*) has already excluded manifest consciousness, the word "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) in the subsequent phrase should be removed. Answer: The very term "manifestation" (*prakhyāna*) explains why that seventh [consciousness] is not a seed.

If it were not so, for what reason would that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) manifesting as the seven [categories] not be called "seeds"? If that were the case, why does the treatise not say "manifesting" (*prabhāsvara*)? Answer: If one were to say "manifesting," one would obtain only one meaning and lose the other two meanings; therefore, it does not say "manifesting. Question: Does "manifesting" then exclude all active functioning (*samudācāra*)?

Question: Why is it that [the seventh consciousness] alone lacks intrinsic nature? Answer: For others, the present [consciousnesses] lack other [factors], and it is not merely this one [that is absent].
As for the seventh, which lacks intrinsic nature, it is only this one factor that is missing;
therefore, it is singled out specifically.
Commentary:
Regarding those that currently exist only as causes—[it is asked: since the essence of the produced fruit-dharma is not non-existent, it cannot fail to arise from a cause.
Why is it that there exists a cause that functions alone? Answer: It is because not all produced effects possess [a corresponding cause].
For example, the object of a solitary image (pratibimba) may exist as a cause of the same kind as its seeing, even if it is not non-existent.
Therefore, the statement that "present existence" refers only to the cause, or alternatively applies to both cause and effect,
is not contradictory; for in the commentary, these are merely assigned to specific or general categories of phenomena respectively.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement "being equally present in the present is also not contradictory," although the cause exists in the state of arising while the fruit exists in the state of ceasing, they are nonetheless simultaneous.
However, since they are both equally present,
this does not contradict the principle that the fruit co-exists with its cause.
According to the third reason below, the cause resides in cessation while the fruit resides in arising.
In this regard, there is an error in the commentary. The commentary states:
"If that is so, regarding the seed in relation to the seed, etc."
The causal seed exists in cessation, while the resultant seed exists in arising.

It should follow that the manifestation of the same seed is called "simultaneous existence with the result" (*phala-sahabhū*). If this were so, what would be the fault? If it were thus, the seed would produce the manifestation.
What is the difference between the two types of seeds in the present life?
Since both are equally results and causes, the commentary concludes by asking: "How is this to be distinguished? Furthermore, this contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that "the manifest and the seeds are of different types," the question is:
for what reason was the Vibhajyavādin previously challenged?
Question: Are their natures and characteristics the same? Answer: Regarding the terms "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) and "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), their natures and characteristics are the same;
this does not refer to all cases. Alternatively, according to that school’s tenet, the substance of the mind itself is designated as the "seed."

The commentary states: "Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to manifestation (*pratyakṣa*). This is not the same as the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*) [discussed] within our own school.
Regarding the statement that "the seeing-part takes the seeing-part as its object," this refers to the self-witnessing-part taking the seeing-part as its object; thus,
the essence of the seeing-part is also called the "seeing-part."
Commentary:
As for that which is not subsumed under the category of cause and condition:
although seeing and that which is seen are simultaneously designated as cause and effect, [they are not so in this context].
It is not a cause-and-condition [relationship].
Commentary:
If that is so, regarding the seed in relation to its manifestation and so forth...
"Similarity of kind" refers to the category of seeds;
however, this is merely cause and effect and is not termed "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
[Commentary:]
Regarding the statement "because it is not permitted for a later seed to produce a fruit," this concludes the refutation of causelessness;
for if the latter were able to produce the fruit from the former, [it would follow that there is no causal sequence].
There may be causes and conditions;
yet, since many things arise together while there is nothing that actually arises,
there are no causes and conditions.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement, "The same should apply to seeds in relation to their types," this means that although they are of the same category, there are no two distinct substantial entities (*svabhāva*) among their actual manifestations; thus, they are attained simultaneously in a single moment. Question: Are not the two kinds—the original and the newly acquired—simultaneous? Answer: If they were simultaneous as causes and conditions, it would be impossible.
Since the original and the new are not causes [of one another], there is no fault.
If that were so, even if a new seed were to produce a manifest state,
it would likewise not be a causal condition for the manifest state of the original seed.

Why do you not allow them to coexist? Answer: Because two minds cannot coexist in a single moment. If that were so, then new seeds of matter (*rūpa*) should arise as manifest phenomena, since there are many [seeds] coexisting that do not obstruct the manifestation of matter.
Answer: Because the conditions (*pratyaya*) have not yet been assembled.
Furthermore, if [arising] were existent, there would be the fault that it has not yet been exhausted.
Commentary:
Question: If that is so, up to the point where it contradicts the essential nature (tattva).
The intent of this objection is as follows:
the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) should likewise produce new seeds through accumulation;
it should not arise with the simultaneous, originally existing seeds as its cause.
Commentary: Regarding the point that these do not occur simultaneously, which would result in the fault of [the seed] reaching the seed and producing the seed; this refers to the following.
The meaning of this explanation is as follows:
these seeds produced by the massed [aggregates] are induced by the untainted seeds that arise simultaneously with the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma);
they do not arise from untainted seeds that are simultaneous with themselves.
Therefore, there is no fault of seeds arising from seeds of the same momentary thought.
Question:

Why is this mass-produced seed called "newly perfumed"? Answer: Because by the power of the perfuming of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), uncontaminated seeds (*anāsravabīja*) are increased.
The untainted seeds induce subsequent *piṇḍa-bhava* (embodied existence).
It is for this reason that *piṇḍa-bhava* receives the designation "newly perfumed.
[Commentary].
Regarding the claim that "only three dharmas exist as original seeds":
this refers to the view that both original seeds and newly manifested [dharmas] together act as causes and conditions to produce newly perfumed seeds.
This is not a correct explanation.
Because the original seed is not a causal condition for the new [seed],
there is no logical fault even if one considers it a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*).
[End of] Commentary.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of this prātimokṣa, etc.":
by virtue of this identical mindfulness that lacks the seeds for the production of [new] aggregates,
it serves as a superior support for the previously attained prātimokṣa vows.
Commentary:
Regarding the previous explanation that "the essence increases,
etc.," this refers to the meaning of the four dharmas being simultaneous.
Regarding the statement,
"Although cause and effect ultimately lack intrinsic nature," some offer this objection:
Because present causes have functional effects that are not non-existent,
it can be said that the effect arises from a present cause. However,
when the effect exists in the future, its substance does not yet exist.

How can a present effect arise from a cause? Answer: It is precisely because the subsequent effect has no [prior] location that one can say it arises from a cause. Objection: Since the substance of the cause has already perished, while its activity remains constant, one may say that the effect arises from the activity of the cause.
When the substance of the cause perishes, its activity ceases accordingly;
thus, a subsequent fruit would not arise in the absence of a cause. Regarding this, there is an interpretation as stated below:
one observes that present phenomena possess an activity that projects a subsequent state.
The present cause is spoken of in contrast to the provisionally established future fruit;
therefore, the present cause is able to project the subsequent fruit. [The opponent] refutes this, saying:
"This is not so. In this sense of 'seed,' cause and effect arise in succession, and both are real."
They claim that the manifest consciousness is a mere designation for cause and effect;
one should not use this to prove the present point. To examine this:
other interpretations contradict reason as previously refuted regarding the production of a subsequent fruit from a prior cause; now, I shall briefly respond.
Since a past cause gives rise to a subsequent effect,
if the cause were non-existent, the subsequent effect could not arise;
yet the essence and function of the present cause are clearly not non-existent.
If the subsequent effect arises from a cause, what fault is there?
Other difficulties should be considered by analogy.
[End of] Commentary.
Since the cause is understood to include both seeds and the possession of seeds:
the former seed serves as the cause for the present activity,
while the latter seed serves as the cause for subsequent seeds.
The seeds capable of producing [future] seeds are called "seeds of existence" (*bhava-bīja*); alternatively, those seeds currently capable of perfuming are called "seeds of existence.
These seeds serve as the cause for this "seed of existence."

This clarifies that the seed and the manifest, as well as the two [the manifest and the seed], serve as causes for one another. Question: According to the second chapter of the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā*, the commentary on the citation regarding "one's own fruit" asks:
"Now, of what is this seed the seed?"
The answer is: it can only project its own fruit.
Regarding the term "only":
if at this time it is capable of producing its own fruit, [then it projects it].
At that very time, it is designated as the "seed.
Since both the seed and that which possesses the seed are beginningless. [Commentary:
"Seed" refers to the *bīja* (seed).
That which possesses seeds is the ālayavijñāna.
Because the ālayavijñāna possesses seeds, it is called "possessing seeds. Furthermore, the cause is termed "seeds," while the fruit is termed "possessing seeds.
The former explanation is superior, because these seeds and the state of possessing seeds both exist from beginningless time prior to the arising of the fruit.

Question: Since the seeds are cited as being named "leading" (ākṣepaka), does the explanation in the Commentary not contradict this? Answer: Although the Commentary employs that [term] "seed" and uses the name "having seeds," its intended meaning is different.
Therefore, there is likewise no contradiction. Regarding the phrase in the Commentary,
"because it is produced by the perfuming agent":

The seed is that which can perfume and produce the present. If this is so, what is the meaning of "original existence" (*prakṛtistha*)? The answer is: it is also due to its increase, or it is called "produced" by way of metaphorical designation based on its characteristics.
Commentary:
As for how Jayasena explains this,
he says there is no fault.
Although the two characteristics of arising and ceasing belong to the same world-period, these two moments are related as cause and effect;
therefore, they are not identical to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
[Commentary].
Furthermore, how is it explained that there is no "already-arisen" [phenomenon] without a seed?
Jayasena explains:
"That is the principle of conformity."
This is not the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, what fault would there be?
A detailed explanation will be provided below.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "the Sarvāstivāda [school] holds that wholesome factors such as *saddharma* act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for unwholesome and neutral [factors]," a question arises:
according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is said:
That is to say, similar dharmas serve as homogeneous causes for similar dharmas.
Regarding the three natures and the five aggregates, they belong to their own category and their own stage;
thus, they act as causes only for those within their own stage and own category.
Question: How can it be said that the wholesome and the unwholesome are of the same category? Answer: The wording of the commentary is general;
its intended meaning is to state that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the unwholesome serves as a cause for the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Because they belong to the same category (*nikāya*). [The Commentary states:
"As for the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and so forth being results of a different nature (*visabhāga-phala*):"
According to the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school,
the two views— the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)— are universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*),
and their essential nature is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
It serves as the cause for all five categories of defiled dharmas belonging to its own level.
Since among these five categories of defilements there are those that are unwholesome (*akuśala*), the cause and effect may thus be of different natures.
If this is so, how can it produce a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*)? Because both are defiled, they are called "uniform outflow."
Commentary:
Regarding the fact that the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) takes the maturation fruit (vipāka-phala) and so forth as its results,
the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

This means that these [factors] share with the mind a single fruit, a single maturation, and a single outflow. Question: Why does the subsequent section state that co-existent and associated [factors] obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)? Answer: Within the fruit of human effort, there is both a general and a specific sense.
The fruit of specific human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is obtained solely through the co-existent (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayuktaka*) causes.
If it pertains to general human effort, it may be obtained through all six causes;
however, any fruit acquired through the exertion of effort is termed a fruit of human effort.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
The commentary relies on the general explanation.
[End of] Commentary.
"What meaning is lacking here?
and so forth constitutes both the question and the answer.
Because these eight [factors] are not capable of perfuming (*vāsanā*), they lack simultaneity with the result (*phala-sahabhū*).
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "those persons who lack the nature [for liberation]," etc.,
this serves as a question based on what preceded.
The eighth [point] concerns the meaning of non-infusion and the coexistence of results.
Since the seventh [point], being infused, possesses all six characteristics,
it should therefore be called a "seed" (*bīja*).
Commentary:
Regarding the eighth section,
this further clarifies the characteristics of causes, which comprise ten sections in total.
The meaning of the seed should be discussed in the eighth [chapter]. Question: It is said that what draws forth its own fruit arises from its respective seeds, such as matter (rūpa) and mind (citta).

How then can the seventh [consciousness], the objective part (nimittabhāga), give rise to the eighth? Answer: Because it is a mental characteristic (cittanimitta), it is able to produce the mind. Question: Are the perfumed seeds one or two? If so, what fault would there be? If there were only a single seed, how could it produce both the deliberative (savitarka) and non-deliberative (nirvitarka) states?
Because there is a distinction between the seven characteristics and the eight views.
If the two types of perfuming agents are indeed one, how can the seeds be two?
Answer: Although the perfuming agent is one, [the seeds are two].
Because there is the essential nature (svabhāva), there is no fault in [the熏]ing of the two;
the rest should be analyzed.
Treatise.
Regarding "external grains, wheat, and so forth":

Question: Since both internal and external seeds are capable of acting as causes, why do you speak only of external [seeds] as being nominal and not actual seeds? Answer: According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asaṅga, this is explained by two verses.
As fully cited in the commentary, the *Anihsvabhāvavāda-ṭīkā* states:
"Furthermore, regarding external seeds such as rice and the like, some may be sown and yet perish;
others, such as weeds and tares, may arise even without being sown."
How is it that internal seeds do not incur the faults of "loss" (*hāni*) and "acquisition" (*prāpti*)—as would occur with external seeds regarding what is produced or not produced?
Therefore, the next response states:
"Thus, there is a contradiction."
Because internal seeds and external seeds are of different natures, they are said to be contradictory.
If there were a distinction between internal seeds and external seeds, [then...]
Why was it stated in the preceding passage that the ālayavijñāna is the true seed of all phenomena?
It was in order to avoid this objection that it was further stated that external seeds have internal [seeds] as their conditions, and so forth.
Since rice and other such things are all transformations manifested through the power of the *ālayavijñāna*,
based on the seeds of karmic perfuming that constitute the objects of experience for sentient beings,
external seeds are not distinct from the internal [consciousness]. Furthermore, Vasubandhu says:
That is to say, external seeds are designated as "seeds" only from the perspective of conventional truth. Why is this?
Because they, too, are all manifestations produced by the ālayavijñāna.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "because it undergoes a profound transformation," when the root-seed has already undergone the eighth transformation and the manifest root arises:
Furthermore, regarding the transformation of the faculties,
the treatise states:
"The power of these seeds produces proximate fruits, and so forth."
Question: Why is it necessary to cite this? Answer: According to the second chapter of the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā* on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which explains this in full detail, it says in brief:
"If these two seeds were merely generative causes (*janaka-hetu*) and not projecting causes (*ākṣepa-hetu*), [the subsequent states would arise without being projected by prior karma]."
If seeds such as wheat were stored in granaries and the like,
they would not continue in a similar succession for a long time;
likewise, after death, the successive states of the corpse, such as the livid discoloration and swelling, would not persist.
What is it that should perish immediately upon death?
How can it be said to perish spontaneously later on?
It is like shooting an arrow: the force exerted when releasing the string acts as the productive cause.
Once the arrow leaves the bowstring, it does not fall immediately.
The exertion applied while bending the bow serves as the propelling cause for the arrow,
causing it to move forward until it reaches its distant destination.
It is not produced solely by the force of the action of releasing the string,
for [the arrow] would immediately fall; nor is it produced by the momentum of motion,
for if they were merely pushing one another in succession, it would not fall.
Since it has already left the string and travels far to reach its destination,
we know that within this process there are two types of force capable of producing and drawing forth [the result].
(Commentary)
If that is so, then why do you not consider conventional phenomena such as emptiness?
This is the objection;
its intended meaning is as follows:
If the provisional were non-existent, there would be no need for such a distinction;
the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should likewise not require a distinction,
because it is subsumed under the term "unconditioned wholesome" (*asaṃskṛta-kuśala*).
Because non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth are co-arising with [their respective causes],
although they are included within the categories of the wholesome and so on, they are further distinguished separately.
Even though provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) do not exist, what fault would there be in negating them?
Commentary:
For this reason, that which should be explained first as "wholesome" is precisely what was stated previously:
that which is dependent on others is a provisional designation.
This interpretation is superior. [The] Commentary [states]:
"Ignorance perfumes the True Suchness," and so forth.
Since ancient times, many of virtuous character have employed this strategy;
this treatise clarifies and simplifies [the matter],
and thus we know that the ancients were not correct.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa also stated that True Suchness (tathatā) receives perfuming and maintains the seeds;
this is likely an error by the translator.
Regarding the phrase "those who lack the nature [for liberation]," etc.:
Question: Even if one does not say that what is defiled is not subject to perfuming, why is this distinction necessary?
Answer: It is precisely the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) that is taken as the substance capable of being perfumed.
Is the seventh [consciousness] not indeed the mind-king (*citta-rāja*)?
It is for this reason that it is distinguished [from the others] solely by its being defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
(Commentary)
As for the fault of a single seed producing two sprouts:
it would be as if a single seed of consciousness were to sustain both form and mind in two locations simultaneously,
since their perfuming occurs at the same time.
Their capacities are also equal;
subsequently, when conditions for arising are encountered, they arise simultaneously in both locations.
Therefore, two consciousnesses arise at one and the same time.

Although there are two bases, because they constitute a single consciousness, they are termed "one kind. If this is so, why does the subsequent objection state that there is the fault of "many kinds producing one"? The answer is: in reality, it is indeed one kind that produces many.
There is the error of generating many [instances] from one;
there is no fault in citing them alternately, whether preceding or following.
Treatise.

Regarding the statement that "those which possess superior efficacy are capable of perfuming," some say that among the six consciousnesses produced by karma, there are those that are superior and those that are inferior; the inferior cannot perfume.
The treatise states that [the inferior] is not perfumed; however,
if this statement that it is "not perfumed" were made as a general rule without any specific qualification,
then the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) would likewise not be included among the perfuming agents (*vāsaka*).
Because it is called "maturation" (vipāka),
we know that only that which is superior can be perfumed by karma.
What, then, is this "superior"?
This refers to the three types of feeling.
Because that which is associated with neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā) is exclusively inferior,
it is not capable of perfuming.
Both painful and pleasant sensations are termed "superior aspects of formations" (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*);
these are capable of perfuming.
Alternatively, within neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), three types may further be distinguished.
Contrary, favorable, and neutral.
The neutral does not perfuse;
the other two are able to perfume. Furthermore, there is another explanation which says:
In this context, only the eighth mental complex is excluded;
for the maturation of the six consciousnesses is never incapable of being perfumed,
as there is no separate scriptural authority stating that they are not perfumed.
The eight [factors] that lack the quality of being perfumed cannot be perfumers.
The six [factors] that possess the quality of being perfumed are without exception perfumers.
Furthermore, if mind and mental factors are not perfumers, they must be the perfumed.
"How can there be a mental factor that is neither the perfumer nor the perfumed? To explain:
both [positions] are unreasonable.
The critique of the first master’s view is as set forth in the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning).
Furthermore, regarding the distinction between superior and inferior based on the three types of feeling (*vedanā*),

since this is not found in the sacred teachings, is it not merely a matter of personal opinion? If the latter master says that only the eighth consciousness is excluded while all others are capable of perfuming (*vāsana*), [then...]
This treatise should conclude that only the seven evolving consciousnesses can be perfumers.
Why, then, is it necessary to speak of "superior power and function"?
Since the terms "superior" and so forth are used, it is clear that there is an intentional exclusion.
Furthermore, since the other six consciousnesses possess that which is perfumed (*vāsya*), they should all be capable of perfuming (*vāsaka*).
Likewise, the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the eighth consciousness should also be capable of perfuming, because they too possess that which is perfumed.
Moreover, one might ask: what mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are there that are neither the perfumer nor the perfumed?
The eighth [position], that it is associated [with the mind],
should not be a mental factor (caitta), because it is neither the perfumer nor the perfumed;
since there are thus many fallacies.
Therefore, it cannot be relied upon.
Regarding the phrase "the two kinds of produced [phenomena]" and so forth in the commentary:
This refers to the seeds of self-designation and the seeds of karma.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "or this *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena)," etc.:
Commentary: It is not necessary to refer to what is produced by those two types;
rather, it is simply because [the object] is useless that it cannot be perfumed.
Regarding the phrase "such as wrong views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is asked:
although their categories are the same, there are differences in their increase and decrease;

how can it be that only that which increases is called a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*)? The answer is: when the treatise states that both increase and decrease are called perfuming agents, it means the following.
Whichever of these two exists is itself the perfumer (*vāsanā*).
Otherwise, the untainted (*anāsrava*) states produced from the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) onward would only increase and never diminish, and thus could not function as perfumes.
If that [seed] can still permeate this [consciousness], why is this not accepted?
Regarding the commentary’s question: "Has it not already been established previously that there is a sense in which [defilements] are abandoned all at once yet still possess a 'grasping' (prāpti)?"
"Can one suddenly sever [the afflictions] within the various stages prior to the tenth stage?
This is a hypothetical question.
It is easy to understand that it is not answered.
According to principle, although a Bodhisattva has the power to sever [the afflictions], they intentionally retain them for two reasons:
first, out of deliberate intent;
second, to avoid obstructing the stages (bhūmi).
Therefore, it is certain that there is nothing that the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) does not reach in severing the afflictions of the path of cultivation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "each stage (*bhūmi*) encompasses what is to be severed throughout the three realms": [this refers to the fact that the diamond-like concentration of each stage simultaneously severs all remaining afflictions of the three realms belonging to that stage].
This statement is inverted.
Its intended meaning is that within each individual stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the three realms.
[Commentary].
Regarding the nine grades:
the nine stages of the three realms are combined into nine grades;
it is not that each individual stage separately possesses nine grades.
Commentary:
"The previous explanation is established" means that the first interpretation of the meaning of "only increasing" is thereby validated.
Therefore, the Commentary itself states that "today it is increased," clarifying that the preceding second interpretation is not established.
Question: Although the objects of perception within the three realms are no different, the aspect of the perceiving consciousness acts solely as a single, constant [perception].

What other cause is there for the establishment of the nine grades? Answer: As ignorance gradually increases, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the three realms that there are nine grades of differentiation.
What fault is there in this?
Commentary.
If one were to claim that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) based on the seventh [consciousness] and so forth,
this would demonstrate that the second explanation mentioned previously is irrational.
To examine this second explanation in detail:

One should not apply the characteristics of existence and non-existence as analogies for one another, because other [commentaries] offer this interpretation; therefore, I shall set it forth and refute it. Question: Between the two interpretations in the *Śū*, which is superior? Answer: The first interpretation is superior.
The meaning of increase is clearly manifest;
whereas, according to the second interpretation, the meaning of decrease is difficult to discern,
even though the three realms differ in terms of subject, object, and so forth.
Why would there be a diminution of its characteristics?
Therefore, it is the foremost and supreme.
(Commentary)
If one asks what dharma acts as an obstacle when the image-part (nimittabhāga) is mutually perfumed,
there is no dharma that obstructs it and prevents it from being transformed as the perfuming of the image-part;
since such obstructing dharmas do not exist, [it proceeds].
Therefore, it is perfumed. Regarding the phrase "such as the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*)":
[this refers to the fact that the self-verifying portion is perfumed by the image-portion].
If that is so, why does it say that "the seeing [part] perfumes the image [part]"? Answer: This is stated in terms of their functional aspects.
The Commentary states: "This is no obstacle, as it is the same for the fundamental consciousness."
It is explained that within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the seeds giving rise to actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*) are called "simultaneous causes" (*sahabhūhetu*).
This is the same for this [system of] Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
[Commentary].

Regarding the statement, "Because the substance of the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) reaches a point where it cannot be perfumed," this concludes that the substance of the cause in the Hīnayāna is not a co-existent cause. The term "cannot be perfumed" explains the reason why.
Thus, by means of one's own position, the error of others is exposed. The *Śāstra* states:
"It is not the case that the present [dharma] takes the present as its cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) when subsumed under the category of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)."
It is not that which is currently manifesting that serves as a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) with respect to what is presently manifesting.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The question is posed based on the meaning":
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the meaning of essence (*svabhāva*).
Since it is unknowable and lacks a distinct essence, it is not inquired about.
[Commentary].
Regarding the subsequent explanation that follows the verse:
it is called "subsequent" because it occurs after the inquiry.
The phrase "cannot be known" refers to the root verse itself.
Commentary:
Regarding the statement that the *Abhidharma* (Dharma of Enumeration) omits [this] because it refers only to what has been attained (*prāpta*),
that treatise says:
For what purpose is "appropriation" (upādāna) observed?
It means that matter which serves as the basis for the arising of sensation is the meaning of appropriation.
If sensation arises in dependence upon this matter, it is called appropriation.
Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "the sounds and so forth produced by the non-separate great elements," since the four great elements are already grasped as objects by the eighth [consciousness], [they are not separate from it].
Therefore, that which is produced by it is not separate from the great sound and is also called "appropriated" (*upātta*).
The commentary states:
"It is like a hair-net (*keśonduka*)."
The objects of perception are like magical illusions;
because conditioned phenomena are unreal, they are likened to a mass of floating hairs. Some say:
It is said that the object is subtle,
or because the objects are numerous; therefore,
it is compared to the appearance of a mass of hairs.
Commentary:
It is not so that the association of mind and mental factors constitutes their object (*ālambana*).
If it were the case, then—as previously reconciled—the four aggregates would not be designated as "name" (*nāman*).
Since "mind" (*citta*) is defined as that which gathers [the mental factors], it should be the object of the *ālayavijñāna*.
The same applies to the other characteristics. Alternatively, there may be a scribal error;
the character "or" (*huo*) should likely be "how could" (*qǐ*).
The previous explanation is the primary one. Regarding the commentary’s phrase,
"because of the attachment of the mind to that which is grasped," etc.:
Wholesome and indeterminate minds are the conceptualizing agents (*parikalpaka*).
These are the falsely grasping minds,
and the objects grasped by them are designated by the names derived from those very grasping subjects.
That which is grasped by one's own views perfumes the seeds of characteristics;

this may also be termed the "habitual tendencies of false attachment to the thoroughly imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva-vāsanā*). Alternatively, it may be that [the grasper] perfumes the seeds of what is grasped within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the pervasive imagination.
The seeds that are grasped are called "grasping habitual tendencies" (*parigraha-vāsanā*).
The former explanation is superior.
(Commentary).
Regarding the statement that "all forms up to those that should not be objects of cognition":
form is neither an infuser (*vāsaka*) nor a cognizer (*parikalpaka*);
furthermore, it lacks grasping (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, within this objective aspect (*nimitta*) there is no seed; thus,
the eighth consciousness should likewise not take this aspect as its object,
because it is said that [the eighth consciousness] takes the seeds of grasping as its object.
If it is argued that although [the seeds] are real, they take form (rūpa) as their object—
provisionally relying on the theory of seeds to say they take the habitual tendencies of grasping (upādāna-vāsanā) as their object—
then what prevents them from actually taking the seeds of the three natures (tri-svabhāva) as their objects?
Furthermore, speaking in terms of the seeds of defilement,
the commentary asks:
"If that is so, should the eighth consciousness also be capable of perfuming?"
This refutes the underlying misconception.
The proponent of that misconception states:
"Since it is said that the eighth consciousness takes the habitual tendencies of grasping as its object..."
"Why is there no grasping?"—
thus arises this objection.
Commentary.
Regarding the claim that this serves as proof:

it may be acceptable to use the fact that the perfumed seeds are called "grasping habitual tendencies" (upādāna-vāsanā) as proof for the perfuming consciousness being "grasping. However, [the argument] is not tenable.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is not like that.
What is the proof for this? Answer: Other wholesome minds and so forth are called "grasping" because they possess two aspects;
since the storehouse consciousness is likewise, why would it not have grasping?

Therefore, it can serve as the basis for proof. If that were so, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) should also be able to act as a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*), just like the other seven consciousnesses.
Answer: It is not distinct from that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*), nor is it subsumed under the category of a perfuming agent.
(Commentary).
Now, regarding the intention of this master, which will become clear as one proceeds,
he first explains that self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), seeing (*darśana*), and the aspect (*ākāra*) belong to the same category;
subsequently, he explains their distinct categories.
There are many questions and answers,
which will be set forth in detail later.
[End of] Commentary.
If that is so, one should consider how this principle applies to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
According to that treatise, it states:
"Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one takes as an object a limited and narrow apprehended sphere (*ālambana*)."
Within the form realm, it takes as its object vast apprehended spheres;
within the formless realm, in the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, it takes as its object immeasurable apprehended spheres.
In the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one takes as object a subtle apprehended realm;
in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one takes as object an extremely subtle apprehended realm.
How can it be said that these take formless (*ārūpya*) vastness as their object? Answer: This is an error on the part of the textual editor.
The intent of the commentary is to raise an objection based on the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Since consciousness in the formless realm takes only seeds as its object,
[the opponent argues that] it has already been stated that this consciousness takes as its objects of appropriation (*upādāna*) such things as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

It is clearly known that the eighth [consciousness] has the function of taking seeds as its object. Question: Why are those seeds called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and so forth? Answer: Because they are perfumed by mental factors (*caitta*) whose objects are immeasurable, they are thus called "immeasurable"; alternatively, it refers to the functional capacity residing upon the seeds of the immeasurables and so forth.
Because it is able to give rise to immeasurable active mental states (*samudācāra-citta*),
the previous explanation is superior.
(Commentary).
Regarding the phrase "that which is able to produce [results] up to not contradicting the fundamental consciousness":
although that seed possesses many distinct capacities—
namely, being wholesome and being vast— [it functions as such].
Because its vast capacity is of the same nature as indeterminate consciousness,
it is able to take [objects] as its cognitive objects;
"vast" refers precisely to this functional capacity.
This refers to the seed itself. Regarding the commentary’s statement,
"Furthermore, the vast function of the formless realm," etc.:

This explanation should be accepted as correct, for it avoids various faults. According to one interpretation, [the mind] takes the substance of the seeds as its object; as long as they possess functional capacity, all such seeds can be taken as objects. Why is this so?
If it is argued that the specific functional capacity of wholesome seeds is said not to have an object-condition because of its nature,
then the seeds perfumed by both outflowing (sāsrava) wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] would all necessarily pertain to both natures.
Its substance is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while its function is divided into the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Since this is not the case [for the object],

how can it be said that the substance is identical to the indeterminate fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and that this [consciousness] is stated to have it as its objective support (*ālambana*)?
Is it not the case that [wholesome factors] such as those associated with the wholesome are also [wholesome] by way of their function (*kāritra*) rather than their object (*ālambana*)?
If you say that because the substance (*dravya*) is of one kind while the functions are distinct, they thus pertain to both natures,
then when the treatise states that cause and effect are both wholesome, does this refer solely to their function?
Furthermore, the essence (svabhāva) of the seeds of the wholesome and so forth, which is not separate from consciousness, is termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Since their function (vṛtti) is not separate from their essence, it follows the indeterminate nature of that essence.
Therefore, both the essence and the function of these seeds are objects of cognition for consciousness.

Both the essence (*tǐ*) and the function (*yòng*) are produced by that which is wholesome (*kuśala*), etc.; that which can produce the wholesome, etc., is likewise subsumed under the wholesome, etc. Question:

If this is so, would states such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) not all have objects of cognition (*ālambana*)? Answer: They do not have objects of cognition. Question: If that is the case, why is it said that they all "take an object" solely on the basis of their functional capacity (*kāritra*)? Explanation: It is because the functional capacity of the mind to prevent [defiled thoughts] within the seeds of the mind that is weary [of existence] is what constitutes the attainment of non-conception; it is not the attainment itself [that has an object].
It is merely based on this [seed] that one can provisionally designate that meditative concentration.
Although it takes as its object the specific functional capacity of the seed and does not take the provisional [entity] as its object,
nevertheless, that provisional phenomenon is not separate from the real.
When taking the seeds as the condition, one also takes the provisional person [the pudgala] as the condition;
thus, there is no fault. To explain in detail:
since the principles do not follow a single path, how could this meaning not exist?
Upon carefully examining the intent of the commentary, it is indeed without contradiction;
yet, your objection appears to be superficial.
The reason for this is as follows.
Regarding the statement that the nature [of dharmas] is determined based on the fundamental consciousness and in relation to cause and effect:
this is discussed from the perspective of the substance of the seeds (*bīja*) and not from the perspective of their functioning.
Thus, the two natures of wholesome and unwholesome are established through their respective functions.
Why wait for cause and effect before something is designated as wholesome or unwholesome?
Furthermore, since the nature of the seeds follows that of consciousness and their causal character is not constant,
how can one demand that wholesome and unwholesome seeds be definitively restricted to only two natures?
Furthermore, because the substance of the seed is not separate from consciousness, it is termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
If one then objects that the function of the seed must also be indeterminate because it is not separate from the substance of the seed,
then it would follow that the seeds of form are also without material resistance, since they too are not separate from consciousness.
Since the manifest fruit of the form-seed does not depart from the seed, it should lack material obstruction;
yet, because essence and function, cause and effect, are neither identical nor separate, this being so, how could that be otherwise? Furthermore, it says:
If it is argued that the "function of the seeds of aversion" (in states such as the attainment of non-conception) is merely nominal and thus not an object of cognition,
then that attainment would be entirely devoid of substance;
for the function of the seeds of aversion is neither a conditioned entity nor a mere designation.
The preceding treatise states that even the conventional (*prajñapti*) can negate.
To what phenomenon does "the conventional" refer?
Furthermore, regarding the prevention of those who would establish [a position] as being fixed:
Is concentration itself the capacity?
Or is it that concentration is only metaphorically established based upon the capacity?
If concentration were identical to the capacity...
How is meditative concentration (*samādhi*) provisional?
If it were based on that which establishes [the object], there would be the fault of infinite regress;
therefore, we know that concentration is itself the capacity to prevent [distraction].
It is not a determinate consciousness of a specific object;
because it is determinate, it is designated as "provisional.
The fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) does not take [such objects] as its conditions, and thus it is not considered provisional. Furthermore, it says:
If seeds are conditioned by conditions and the conventional is also conditioned by conditions,
then the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) must undergo differentiation and transformation;
through this, the principle of the *Śāstra* becomes logically consistent.
Commentary:
Furthermore, regarding the three grades of seeds:
the seeds of mind, form, and so forth—distinguished by their three natures (trisvabhāva)—each have three grades.
Alternatively, the seeds of the three realms are termed the "three categories. Regarding the commentary's phrase "that which is one's own substance":
it refers to that which constitutes one's own essential nature.
The commentary states: "The characteristic not being separate from consciousness is called its own essence.
As for whether it is severed or not severed, it increases or decreases accordingly."
It is diminished but not increased;
this is the difference in the objects of focus for ordinary beings and noble ones at the eighth [stage].
Commentary:
Regarding the "body possessing faculties" (*sendriya-kāya*),
there is one interpretation that the very substance of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) is what is meant by "possessing faculties."
There is no other capacity [to serve as a faculty].
This is like the term "possessing form" (*rūpin*);
although the entities such as the physical bases (*āśraya*) are not themselves faculties, they are so designated.
That which possesses faculties is also called "possessing faculties. Because the faculties and that which possesses faculties are combined and aggregated, it is termed a "body" (*kāya*).
[Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "because the faculties are subtle," etc.:
In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is explained that the faculties and the body are mentioned together.
Because the faculties are subtle, they are not referred to as "faculties" alone;
because the body might be confused with external objects, it is not referred to as "body" alone.
Therefore, by speaking of them collectively, both errors are dispelled. [The] *shu* (commentary) states:
"That is, the five locations of the sense faculties."
That is, the five *anu* (subtle particles).
Commentary:
"Taking the five objects of others as conditions" means...
This refers to the five sense-objects of the other’s body.
Commentary:
Regarding "this which has measure":
The *Pramāṇa* states:
"That which is self-originated cannot grasp other supported atoms,
because it is not of its own internal body."
Regarding the statement in the treatise,
"These two are both that which is grasped and maintained by consciousness," just as with the five external objects:
This meaning of "appropriation" (upādāna) applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
however, there are differences between them regarding its magnitude and scope.

The *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter five, speaks of it solely in terms of the production of sensation (*vedanotpāda*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter fifty-three, explains it in terms of both the basis that sustains and the production of sensation. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
It means that because it is the physical basis for the arising of sensation (*vedanā*), it has the sense of being "appropriated" (*upātta*).
Since sensation arises in dependence upon this physical form, it is called "appropriated. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
If consciousness, by depending upon and grasping [the body], is called "appropriated matter," then what is this?
It is that which consciousness cognizes.
They share the same welfare and are harmoniously integrated in their growth;
furthermore, they serve as the basis for the arising of various sensations.
Conversely, non-appropriated matter is the opposite of this.
The former is narrow and the latter is broad;
these two points distinguish the two treatises.
Regarding the manifestation, seeds, faculties, objects, and their complete correlation, they are explained in detail according to the commentary as follows, based on the Hīnayāna perspective.
Abhidharmakośa, Chapter Two:
The five present sense faculties and the four objects that support them are termed "appropriated" (upātta);
the remainder are non-appropriated (anupātta).
Regarding the meaning of "appropriation" (*upādāna*),
that same treatise states:
"It is that which is appropriated in common by the mind and mental factors."
That which is subsumed as a basis is called "appropriated" (*upātta*),
because it mutually follows along with benefit and harm;
this is what the world refers to as having "sentient contact."
Because one experiences pleasure and so forth when contacted by various conditions, this is identical to the two meanings [of "appropriation"] found in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Furthermore, the nine factors—such as the faculties and their objects—are as explained in the *Abhidharma*. Question: For what reason does the Mahāyāna maintain that only the eighth consciousness is termed "capable of appropriation" (*upādātr*)? Answer: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51: [The text continues with the scriptural citation.]

It is due to five reasons: first, the ālayavijñāna has as its cause the karmic formations created in previous lives, while the evolving consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness have as their cause present conditions, namely the sense faculties, objects, and so forth;

second, the three moral natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral) are observable in the six consciousnesses; third, the category of the non-obscured-neutral maturation-result (*vipāka*) is not observable in the six consciousnesses; fourth, the six consciousnesses each have their own respective supports, and they evolve based upon those respective supports.
That which serves as their basis would necessarily be appropriated,
while the others would be non-appropriated;
even if one were to grant that it is appropriated, it would still be illogical.
Because consciousness is detached [from the body], (5) furthermore, the basis [of consciousness] would incur the fault of being repeatedly appropriated. Why is this?
Because that visual consciousness arises only at a single time.
At one time it does not transform;
the other consciousnesses are likewise.
Because the eighth consciousness differs from them, it is able to grasp and maintain [the body].
Commentary:
"Transformation" (bian) refers to "transmutation" (zhuanbian),
which is precisely "arising-transformation" (shengbian).
The sub-commentary concludes by stating: "Therefore, the productive cause is called 'capable transformation' (nengbian).
One should understand that the remote condition for the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) is analogous to this.
This means that within the causal state, the eighth consciousness lacks both types of transformation with respect to the untainted seeds.
Because they do not take [objects] as conditions and are not perfumed, they are respectively not termed "evolving from conditions" (*pratyaya-ja*) or "transformations" (*pariṇāma*).
At the stage of fruition, the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is termed a "transformation" because it takes [objects] as conditions.
In the causal stage, the untainted (*anāsrava*) sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess both types of transformation.
Regarding the statement that "the seven consciousnesses within the fruit-stage only take names as their objects," the meaning can be understood through reflection.
[End of] Commentary.
Regarding the statement that the faculties, seeds, and so forth possess the two meanings of transformation:
the manifest eighth consciousness, in relation to the faculties and seeds, possesses both conditions and grasps both;
whereas the external vessel-world possesses only the condition.
The seed-consciousness undergoes only one transformation in relation to the seven manifest consciousnesses;
there are no transformations in either direction between the manifest [consciousness] and the seven manifest [consciousnesses].
If the seed-consciousness is considered in relation to the manifest sense-faculties and the vessel-world, [it likewise undergoes only one transformation].
That which arises immediately is called "transformation.
The receptacle world is likewise produced from the seeds of the common characteristics of consciousness.
This commentary merely indicates the general direction by citing the manifest consciousness as an example.
When the manifest consciousness and its seeds are considered together,
the sense faculties undergo three transformations,
while the external vessel-world undergoes two.
Commentary:
Regarding the statement "the Sautrāntika section has been briefly explained," this refers to the Sautrāntika masters [who maintain] that neither arising nor [the other characteristics] exist.
As in the first commentary.
Regarding the phrase "However, only the first interpretation," etc.:

Briefly, there are two explanations. The first states: Just as the eighth consciousness takes its own three objects as conditions but lacks a substantial basis (*nimitta*), the mental factors (*caitta*) take the eight aspects (*ākāra*) as their substantial basis for conditioning.
Alternatively, it may arise by mutually relying on one another as a substrate (*ālambana*).
Therefore, one cannot say that the primary substrate (*mūlālambana*) is identical [to the image] simply because they share the same name.
For this reason, it should be stated that the "characteristic" (*nimitta*) refers to the aspect of the mental formation (*ākāra*).
The first [interpretation] states that "having similar modes of activity" means they share the same object;
the second says this is an error and should instead state: "However, only the second [case] lacks the first understanding.
The remaining words are the same as before. Examination states:
The subsequent explanation clarifies "aspect" (*ākāra*). How is this made clear? Answer:
When one perceives a name as an aspect, although the aspect is merely similar [to the object], because the name is the same as its objective referent (*ālambana*), it is not called an "aspect."
In the end, what is lost? Furthermore, the sub-commentary below cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, stating:
"The *Yogācāra* [treatise] designates them as having the same object (*ālambana*) based on their substantial nature;
this [text], however, designates them as objects based on their reflected images (*pratibimba*)."
How could one possibly treat what precedes and follows as being like Chu and Yue? Furthermore, according to the *Yogācāra-bhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* by the Master of the Commentary:

"If the image (*pratibimba*) is designated as the aspect (*ākāra*), then that which takes the primary object (*bimba*) as its objective support (*ālambana*) would be identical in substance and synonymous in name."
They are called "different" because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct.
If one designates the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as the mode of activity,
then although the essential natures of the [respective] direct object-parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) are each distinct, [the seeing-part remains the same].
Although the name "seeing" (darśana) is the same,
they are called "different" because the substance of the seeing-part and its object are each distinct. For this reason,
it is known that "seeing" refers to the aspect (ākāra).
Regarding the eighth [consciousness], the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is similar in name and shares the same object of cognition;
the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga), however, is distinct for each and thus differs in its mode of activity (ākāra).
If the objective aspect were itself called the "mode of activity," [it would be untenable].
Their modes of activity are identical.
How, then, can it be said that they do not share the same mode of activity?
The eighth [consciousness] does not invariably take the primary object (bhāva) as its cognitive support.
Furthermore, how is it said that they have the same object of cognition (*ālambana*)?
If you say they are called "the same" because their *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) are similar,
then [what of] the object of cognition itself?
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) is one and the same;
how then can one speak of it being "the same" or "different"?
For this reason, it is known that the commentary is erroneous.
Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "because mind and mental factors cannot themselves take themselves as objects," that school does not admit that the dharmas of mind and mental factors can take themselves as their own objects.
Regarding the treatise's statement that "if mind and mental factors reach their respective objects," some masters maintain that the first measure refutes the Saṃmitīyas,
while Sthiramati does not refute other schools.
Now, this interpretation is incorrect.
Although the objects of mind and mental factors possess the characteristic of being traversed when they take an object,
that characteristic of being traversed is the characteristic of the subject that cognizes, not the characteristic of the object that is cognized.
How is it that the first proof refutes only the Saṃmitīya school?
Therefore, it should be stated that the first proof universally refutes all twenty schools. Detailed explanation follows:
Although the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) carried by [the cognition] are reckoned as belonging to the subjective cognizer,
since it is said that these characteristics resemble the object of cognition (ālambana), the object of cognition is itself the characteristic; thus,
the characteristic of the object of cognition is called the "characteristic of the object of cognition" (ālambana-lakṣaṇa).
This is not the same as the Saṃmitīya school; here, even this semblance is absent.
Therefore, what flaw could there be in these virtuous meanings?
[End of] Treatise.
Regarding the statement, "If mind and mental factors lacked the capacity to cognize, etc.," some masters maintain that this refutes the positions of the master Sthiramati as well as Bhāviveka;
however, my current interpretation is that it universally refutes the position of the Saṃmitīya school.
They claim that when the mind and its associates perceive an object, there is no separate mention of the mental aspect (ākāra) within the perceiving mind itself. [The author] examines this, stating:
"This clarifies the two parts."

To say that the characteristic of the object-condition (ālambana-nimitta) is the mind as the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) does not mean it is established based on the seeing-part depending upon the mind.
If it were established separately, how would the three parts be distinguished?
As previously stated, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is termed the "aspect" (ākāra).
How could it be said that this aspect is distinct from the seeing-part itself?
By virtue of this, the valid authority (pramāṇa) possesses the characteristic of being a cognizing subject.
Therefore, it is known that the various masters’ explanations do not contradict the treatise.
[The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Bhāviveka also says," and so forth.
There is another interpretation: according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), not only is there no characteristic of a cognizing subject, but the substance of the mind itself is also non-existent.
This is because the treatise states that both mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) exist.
However, since there is no aspect of a cognizing subject at the time of perceiving an object,
it should be understood that [the refutation] is made solely from the perspective of conventional truth.
All masters say that Bhāviveka maintains that there is an aspect but no seeing.
This does not rely on [our own] tenet,
because that [other system] speaks of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) based on conventional truth;
for within conventional truth, although mind and objects exist, [they are not ultimately real].
"Because the inferior is concealed and the superior is revealed, it is called 'consciousness-only' (vijñaptimātra).
Detailed examination states:
This is not a sound refutation, for it attributes faults to that which is faultless.
Since the Commentary states, "If one relies on the conventional perspective, both the seeing and the object exist," and further says,
"For now, let us set aside your position that everything is solely the object," does this not imply that it allows for the existence of that seeing?
If one says that the refutation of other non-sequential commentaries is applicable to others, yet not to one's own position,
[that argument fails]. The refutation of others may be accommodated, but for what one establishes oneself, it is not so.
Since, according to worldly perception, both [the object and the subject] coexist,
by what reasoning is it that the aspect of the perceiving subject (*ālambaka-lakṣaṇa*) alone is discarded?
Furthermore, is the essence of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*) the manifest (*pravṛtti*) or the seed (*bīja*)?
If that which is currently manifesting lacks a corresponding object of cognition,
how can it be called "manifest consciousness"?
This should be carefully examined.
Commentary:
Regarding the second point, the combined refutation of Sthiramati,
there is another interpretation which states:
In this context, the meaning of Sthiramati’s position is refuted.
Although it is understood that this text [states] "this is two-fold,
not three-fold," how can it be said that he lacks the capacity for the cognitive subject (*ālambaka*)?
Since self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is precisely the function of the subjective aspect (*grāhakākāra*),
one may therefore refute only that [aspect] which lacks the characteristic of an object (*ālambananimitta*) within the two parts. Alternatively,
it may be that this passage does not concern the meaning of the two parts.
This refers to the three parts. In detail:

this clarifies that the two parts—the seeing [aspect] and the image—are designated as the "subject" (ālambaka) and "object" (ālambana) respectively, in order to refute the faults inherent in the position of Sthiramati.
Furthermore, because the treatise itself concludes that mind and mental factors must necessarily possess two aspects,
they cannot be categorized as belonging to the three parts [of the dependent nature].
(Commentary)
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Mahāsāṃghika school [is] equal to this," this explains the meaning of the previously stated nineteen schools.
(Commentary)
"Those who take their own objects as the essence are not like this" indicates the aforementioned "other great assemblies.
(Commentary).

Regarding the phrase "because it has never been a phase-part (nimittabhāga) to be apprehended by the seeing-part (darśanabhāga)," this means that because various forms and so forth have previously served as phase-parts and were apprehended by the seeing-part, they can later be recollected;
since the mind is not like this, [it cannot be recollected].
"How can there be recollection later?
Therefore, the fact that one can recollect later clarifies that it is based on self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) at the prior time.
— Commentary.
Regarding the phrase "the third [chapter],
the Buddha-ground," according to that treatise, it cites the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*,
which states: "The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* says..."
All minds and mental factors are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because they realize their own intrinsic natures.
Were it otherwise, one would not be able to recollect them, just as one cannot recollect what has never been seen.
(Commentary)
Regarding the phrase "In this context, those whose modes of activity reach [the object] are called 'similar'":
this is a further explanation to clarify the intent of that yoga. As for the term "in this context," it refers to this *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The aspect-part (nimitta-bhāga) itself is designated as the "mode of activity" (ākāra). Regarding the statement that the object is spoken of in its totality:
this is because the aspect-part is similar [to the object];
for example, when perceiving blue and so forth, the aspect-part is likewise blue.
Therefore, it is called "collective.
For this reason, the treatise states: "The same object of cognition (*ālambana*).

As for the statement that they are "similar" because their aspects (*ākāra*) are based on distinctions, "similarity" here carries the sense of being "not identical"; thus the treatise says: "different aspects. Question: Now, regarding what is called "similarity," although the entities are not identical, there is some degree of analogy.

Question: What characteristics are seen that cause it to appear similar? Answer: It is like the case where the subject (the mind) and its objects—such as blue and so forth—are all likewise [cognized];
therefore, they are called "similar. Some say:

Regarding the passage "The object [is established] based on the four lines below," the commentary below provides a dual reconciliation of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratā-siddhi*. A detailed explanation states: "It is not so."
The previous explanation is correct;
one may verify this by investigating it.
[End of] Commentary.

Regarding the statement that "this mind and its mental factors are admitted to have an equal basis for as long as they endure," the third fascicle of this treatise says, "the object of cognition and so forth.
The term "and so forth" (等) also carries the meaning of "similarity."
The remainder of the text is the same as that which follows.
Regarding the commentary (*śāstra*): "Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the result of inference (*anumāna*)," and so forth, the questions and answers are likewise.

Question: What is the difference between this question-and-answer session and the previous one, such that it must be pointed out? Answer: The previous [session] was based on a difficulty regarding the divisions;
this is based on a difficulty regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Commentary.
Regarding the "Chapter on Manas":
this refers to the section explaining manas in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
which is designated as the "Chapter on Manas" because it extensively analyzes [the subject] through various thematic categories (*arthamukha*).
The intention behind this commentary is to address the following objection:
"If the five consciousnesses are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can they be bound?"
Therefore, the commentary answers:
"Because it is a state defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), there is bondage.
An external objection is raised:
How is this clearly known?
Therefore, I refer to that chapter.
Now, according to the first treatise of Vasubandhu (Asvabhāva), it says:
This is the basis for the defilement of consciousness;
because it functions constantly and without contradiction throughout all states, whether determinate or indeterminate, virtuous and so forth.
What does "how so" mean? It means that even during moments of wholesome consciousness, one still clings to a self;
by virtue of this, the five sensory consciousnesses come to possess the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*).
To say that this refers to the "Manas Chapter" of the Subcommentary (*Śāstra*) is incorrect. In the Subcommentary, it states:
"That which takes self-cognition as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*)."
This statement is made because function is not separate from its essence. The commentary states:
"The attainment of attainment is the non-attainment of dharmas."
Because there is both great attainment and small attainment,
the word "attainment" is repeated.
This refers to what is attained.

The essence of this dharma is neither the acquisition of a name nor the acquisition of the dharma itself. What is the intention behind the objection? The answer is as follows: just as that "great acquisition" (mahāprāpti) can acquire both the fundamental dharma and the "small acquisition" (anuprāpti), a fourth [acquisition] is not established.
Arising is also like this; the examples are seen to be the same as those [previously given].
For the objective aspect (*nimitta*) and self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), a fourth [consciousness] is not required.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "there is no arising from a separate seed," this follows the interpretation of the Master [Vasubandhu] concerning the similarity of seeds between the aspect (nimitta) and the vision (darśana).
Alternatively, this may be explained as referring to "images-only" (*pratibimba-mātra*) rather than as an exhaustive statement of principle. As for the treatise stating,
"Whether internal or external, all have an object of apprehension (*grāhya*)," etc.:
As clearly explained in the Commentary (Śūtra),
there is one interpretation that agrees with the Commentary,
yet it establishes its reasoning as follows:
The previous long passage states: "That is to say, the second part [of the Buddha's mind] takes only the first as its object.
However, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the Buddha’s mind does not take only the initial [moment] as its object;
it also extends to the subsequent ones."
Furthermore, the preceding thesis explained that contaminated consciousness is not uncontaminated; moreover,
in the uncontaminated state,
all three parts are able to take the other three parts as their objects.
How are the internal and external mutually interconnected?
The Commentary states:
"Although it takes True Suchness as its object, up to the point that it cannot take it as an object."
Although there are passages stating that the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) takes suchness as its object,
since the seeing-part functions externally,
it cannot actually take it as an object. To explain in detail:
Furthermore, the claim that the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) does not take suchness as its object is made merely to conform to the convention of calling this seeing-part "external";
it does not fully accord with the ultimate principle.
Commentary:
"If that were so, the internal mind would not be the external fruit.
The intent of this objection is as follows:
There is a distinction between the internal and the external.
The external is not the fruit of internal dharmas;
the meanings of "external" and "internal" are different.

"Internally, it is also not the fruit of the external. Answer: This refers back to the previous argument; the meaning of "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*) can be understood through reflection. Now, he answers again:
"The single act of seeing universally takes both the internal and external as its objects, which is a contradiction."
