Therefore, the external [consciousness] does not serve as the fruit of the internal dharma;
since the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga) lacks both faults,
the internal [consciousness] can indeed serve as the fruit of the external.
Commentary:
If the mind were to take itself as its own object, it would fall into the error of being non-distinct [from its objects];
that is, the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) would then be taking the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) and so forth as its objects.
Based on this, one may raise the following objection:
since both the agent and the object are equally of the nature of mind, there is no distinction between them.
Some say that this objection is raised from the perspective of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and not from the perspective of the fourfold division [of consciousness].
If all is merely consciousness, how can there be distinctions such as cause and effect? To this, we reply in detail:
It is not so; for these difficulties arise only when one fails to discern the four fundamental aspects of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The sub-commentary concludes by stating that this is explained according to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).
Thus, it is known that this is not a critique based on the difficulty of the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) theory.
Regarding "the external primary elements" (*bāhya-mahābhūta*):
there is one interpretation which states that the term "external" serves to distinguish them from the internal.
There are five explanations for the distinction between the internal and the external: first, it is said that what is grasped [as an object] is called "external."
That is to say, because it is external to the mind, everything else is called internal;
for it is not separate from consciousness. Second, the objective essence (bimba) is called external.
Furthermore, because they are external to the mind, reflections are called "internal," as they exist within one's own mind.

Third, it is said that the distinctions between the meanings and principles of all phenomena are called "internal," while the substantial entities and intrinsic natures of those phenomena are called "external."

Therefore, those who are confused about the principle say that [actions] based on the internal gate are called "internal," while the initiation of body, speech, and so forth is called "based on the external. Fourth, it is said that what exists within one's own continuum is termed "internal."
The bodies of others and non-sentient things are called "external," because they are all external to one's own body.
The fifth [treatise] states that among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six sense faculties (*indriya*) which serve as the central support are called "internal."
Because they are proximate,
the six objects that serve as the focal points for the mind and its associates are called "external," due to their relative remoteness.
The present treatise states that "external" refers to the fourth category.
However, the commentary says: "Although it is not external to consciousness, it is called 'external' by virtue of being an external base (*bāhyāyatana*).
This interpretation is incorrect.

Since the treatise itself states that both the faculties (*indriya*) and their bases are collectively termed "internal," if one were to categorize them according to the system of bases (*āyatana*), the faculties could indeed be called internal, while the physical supports for the faculties would have to be called external. A detailed examination states: [The faculties] and their bases are both designated as "internal" because the treatise itself declares them so together.

If one were to apply the classification of the bases (*āyatana*), the faculties could be classified as internal, whereas the physical supports for the faculties would necessarily be classified as external. Therefore, [the text] says: "A detailed examination states..."
I have severed my own misconceptions;
this commentary is free of contradiction.
It simply states that because the sense-bases (āyatana) of form and so forth arise from external conditions, they receive the designation "external."
Who says that it encompasses the "color that supports dust"?
This is because it arises in a location distinct from the sound.
Furthermore, since it relies on the fourth dhyāna of another's body, how could it be the same as the external vessel-world?
The intent of the treatise is solely to clarify the matter of external material forms (*bhājana-rūpa*).
If it is argued that only a portion of the fourth [dhyāna] is taken, why exclude the fifth?
Since there is no distinction made regarding the fourth, this argument is self-refuting.
Commentary:
Regarding the two types of "common" [dharmas] among the sixty-six [categories] in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
that treatise states:
Conditioned by wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mental orientations (*manasikāra*), prior karma is activated;
this is able to draw forth the various formations (*saṃskāra*) and cause them to persist without interruption,
namely those arising from external factors produced by common and uncommon karma.
Explanation:
This clarifies that sentient beings abide by means of these three types of karma, which enable them to perceive the receptacle world;
with the receptacle world as their support, sentient beings are able to abide.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "the common and the uncommon are like one's own fields and houses," there is an interpretation that it is subsumed solely by the first clause.
It is mostly for one's own enjoyment;
however, because it also possesses the sense of being enjoyed by others,
it is like the sensory bases (āśraya) which exist only within one's own body.
If even a small portion that serves the purpose of others is still called "shared," how can fields and so forth be termed "unshared" by contrast? To explain in detail:
this is not possible.
If that were so, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) that support the objects should also belong to the first category,
as they serve the purpose of others, like fields or houses.
If you argue that because they belong to oneself they do not belong to the first category, [then the same logic would apply to the sense-faculties].

The same should apply to dwellings and so forth, as they also belong to oneself. If it is argued that the supporting objects (*ālambana*) do not conform to this because they belong to one's own internal body, it is precisely by virtue of this principle that supporting objects are termed "common within the uncommon."
Houses and the like are called "common within the uncommon" because they differ from external things;
furthermore, they do not belong to others.
Therefore, it is not included in the first category. Question: The pure lands manifested by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others do not exist apart from impure realms;
when comparing the pure and the impure, they should correspond to the second category. Regarding this, there are two traditional interpretations.
One interpretation states that [the first sentence] refers to impure contaminated [dharmas], which are similar by virtue of sharing the same location;
furthermore, karma is also partially similar, while the experience of its results differs, hence it is called the second phrase.
The Buddha, however, possesses only uncontaminated [dharmas].
The Bodhisattva is utterly pure;

although they dwell together with those who are defiled, because there is a distinction between pure and impure karma, this is not the second case. Second, it is said that since the location of the pure and the defiled is identical...
This refers to the second type: that which is common yet not shared. The detailed explanation states:
First, "good" (*śubha*) is explained.
For now, consider how the environment and sentient beings of the same level undergo common transformation.
Because there are distinct karmas that further differentiate objects such as houses and so forth within this [realm],
ordinary beings and Buddhas are not like them;
how then could they be considered equivalent under the second category?
Commentary:

Regarding the statement, "When taking length and so forth as objects, one simultaneously takes blue and so forth as objects," there is an interpretation that those which take length and so forth as objects do so by treating them as primary.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the pure lands manifested through the eighteen kinds of perfect purity possess both manifest color and shape.
By analogy, one should understand that the impure lands, which are transformations according to consciousness, also possess color and shape, with their dimensions varying in breadth and narrowness.
The preceding treatise also states: "Regardless of its size, it manifests instantaneously as a single appearance. To examine this:
the statement that it takes length and so forth as its object refers to distinct conditions;
does it mean that length and so forth are not separate from blue and so forth?
When one perceives blue and so forth, it is said that one perceives their objects.
If it has already been clarified that perceiving objects is a remote perception,
then if they were perceived separately, how could the eighth consciousness undergo transformation through causal conditions?
Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the Buddha-ground is not [the same] because of the distinction between pure and impure;
for the treatise states:
"Although all sentient beings, when they reach the state of universality, appear as one."
Question: Suppose, for example, that a single tree is transformed by the collective karma of sentient beings.
When one sentient being cuts it down for use, does he use what was transformed by his own karma, or does he use what was transformed by others as well?
If [the tree] were produced by one's own [consciousness] alone, then when other people undergo a transformation [of consciousness], the tree should continue to exist; why is it not seen?

If it also employs others [as causes], how can it be called "representation-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*)? Answer: Since trees and the like are produced from seeds that are common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), [they appear similarly to all].
All [beings] accord with one another and mutually benefit each other.
For a single sentient being, that which is transformed by itself serves as the direct object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the immediate instrumental cause (*upayoga*).
That which is transformed by others serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for what is transformed by oneself, and thus functions as a remote instrumental cause.
When all things are viewed in relation to one another, that which is itself is the "conformed-to" (anuvidheya), while the other is the "conformer" (anuvidhāyaka).
Since the conformer ceases when there is no longer a conformed-to, it too ceases.

From this, the refutation of the tree [as a real entity] establishes that Vijñapti-mātra is also established. Question: How is it known that they mutually augment one another? Answer: The seventh chapter of the Abhidharma-kośa states that there is collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*) which serves as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As follows, the subsequent passage quotes: "If that were so, the meaning of the analogy of the lamp and its light would not be established.
When the flame of one lamp is extinguished, other lights still remain;
since the phenomena do not correspond, how can it serve as an analogy? Answer: Because the analogy takes up only a partial aspect, there is no contradiction.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "the fifty-four types of dharmas with resistance" (*sapratigha*), the text cited in the commentary is abbreviated; here it is provided in full.
For what reason do all obstructive dharmas occupy the same location without being separated from one another, yet they are not said to possess the nature of non-obstruction?
Answer: Because they function in accordance with one another.
Because they arise in mutual succession and do not obstruct one another,
and because they are produced as such by the predominant influence of these types of threefold karma.
Why is this? Because all aggregates of form and all faculties of form are experienced in common. The commentary explains that the intent of the objection is as follows:

For example, within a single aggregate of matter, other subtle elements such as fragrance and so forth likewise occupy that same location; therefore, they should be called "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*).
The intent of the answer is that among the categories of matter and so forth, there are both those that are obstructive and those that are non-obstructive.
Those who violate [the precepts] shall dwell separately;
those who comply shall dwell together.
Furthermore, this is brought about by the power of karma.
How is it known that there are many [atoms] in a single location?
For example, when a mass of color is seen by the eye as color,
its fragrance is smelled by the nose.
The tongue experiences taste,
and the body perceives touch; therefore,
it is said that the material sense organs (rūpīndriya) are experienced in common.
Commentary:

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "when becoming a vessel, [beings from] the third dhyāna and other realms of other directions [arrive]," this is because the fourth dhyāna is neither destroyed nor newly formed.
Therefore, the treatise merely cites their formation and destruction as occurring in the same location. Consequently, it states:
"Even if one is born in another region or within one's own realm," and so forth.
Question: Since both the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) and the seeds (*bīja*) are objects, why are their conditions not the same?
Answer: The receptacle world serves as a support (*āśraya*) and transforms only within its own level (*svabhūmi*);

the seeds are not like this, for they can be taken as objects across all levels. Furthermore, because the seeds of the three realms follow the realm in which the transforming consciousness (*vijñāna*) resides, they can be perceived accordingly.
The vessel [of the world] is not like this; how can it be used as an analogy?
Commentary:
As for the transformation by Mahābrahmā.
This refers to what is said in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* regarding the Brahmā King:
"I see this world-realm as being like the palace of Maheśvara.
This is precisely that matter.
Furthermore, when gods from the higher realms come to this realm,
they must transform their pure vessels into their own support,
because this coarse realm cannot sustain them.
Commentary:
Regarding the passage from the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Dharma) stating, "up to the fifth [chapter],
because it follows the seeds of karma," I have examined that fifth chapter and found no such textual statement.
In that seventh [chapter], the five types of common karma are clarified;
thus it says: "As the Sūtra states, there is common karma. What is common karma?
It is that karma which causes the various distinctions within the receptacle world."
Furthermore, there are certain karmas that cause sentient beings to act as mutual predominant conditions for one another;
by the power of this karma, it is said that sentient beings stand in relation to each other as predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Because they mutually possess dominant influence (*adhipatibala*), it is also called "common karma" (*sādhāraṇakarma*).
One might suspect that "seven" was erroneously transcribed as "five";
the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Compendium of Abhidharma) also cites this, agreeing with the present treatise.
There is a sūtra that provides scriptural proof for the matter of collective karma; consider this further. [The] Commentary [states]:
"This demonstrates the arising in the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*) and so forth."
The commentary explains that intention by stating that based on karmic seeds, the various distinctions within the receptacle world are termed "common karma" (*sādhāraṇa-karman*).
It does not mean that all [karma] must arise as actualized activity (*samudācāra*) to transform the receptacle world before it can be called common karma.
Commentary:
If it were not so, the meaning of the four divisions would not exist;
for one who does not project a reflected image, having already directly realized the third division through vision, [the subsequent stages follow].
Why is it necessary for the fourth [cognition] to be the result of valid cognition?
Therefore, there are not four parts.
[Commentary].
Regarding the statement that "the seeds of the three natures therein follow consciousness and are not afflictions," some say that although the three natures differ,
they are designated as indeterminate (avyākṛta) according to their basis.
"Afflictions are identical to the unwholesome and so forth;
therefore, they are not termed 'afflictions'. [The author] explains:
"Nature (svabhāva) is defined by the sense of its essential category (jāti)."
They may be indeterminate according to their respective bases.

Because they increase the specific meaning of affliction (*kleśa*), the seeds are termed "afflictions. Question: Since afflictions are not themselves defiled (*kliṣṭa*), can they not be designated according to their bases?
Since they are already subsumed within the two natures, they are not afflictions according to those natures.
Answer: Although their realms and seed-natures are the same, [they differ in that]...
Because they are based on distinct supports or,
likewise, belong to different categories,
they are not designated according to their support.
Between these two explanations, one may choose and adopt according to one’s own inclination. [The *Śāstra*] states:
"Regarding the divine eye and ear up to 'it should not be a sentient being'..."
If one does not admit that the divine eye and ear faculties— which take objects of a different realm as their domain— are distinct from the eight fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
then because the eighth [fetter] would not be sustained by them, it should decay and perish. If this were so,
what would be called a "sentient being"?
Commentary:
Regarding the statement that there would be the fault of sentient beings increasing or decreasing [in number],
the divine eye and the divine ear belong to the category of sentient beings.
Because a separate body arises that does not belong to this [original one], it is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*).

Furthermore, if it becomes rotten and decays, it is also called "decrease" (*hāni*). Question: In terms of the ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*), what is maintained such that there is no fault of increase?
"Because their bonds are different. Answer: Although the bonds are different, they do not depart from this realm;
because there is a consciousness that can maintain them and to which they belong, they are not called "sentient" (*qing*).
(Commentary)
Regarding "the first master among those difficult to refute" and so forth:
this refers to the first master among those of inferior faculties within the body [of the text].
The commentary (*shu*) seizes this opportunity to preemptively challenge his interpretation.
Commentary:
"The same applies to those born blind" means that although they have not fallen into decay or ruin, their sense faculties still remain.
It is only because external objects act as obstructions that one is unable to see;
this is not the case with a withered tree.
Commentary.
Regarding the fourth verse and subsequent verses of the old edition:
it is asked that although the objects and consciousnesses in the old and new verses differ in their sequence,
their general meaning is similar.
"Why is there such a partial censure? Answer: It was formerly called the "fundamental consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*).
Since the fundamental consciousness is restricted to being one, the claim that it "resembles" those [objects] constitutes a fault.
The *Xinyan* states that consciousness arises;
since "consciousness" encompasses the eight consciousnesses, there is no error in [the claim] that it follows conditions such as the self (*ātman*). The *Xinlun* commentary explains:
"Transforming into what resembles objects" means appearing as the nature of various objective spheres such as form and so forth.
"Transforming into what resembles sentient beings" means appearing as the nature of the five sense faculties of oneself and others.
That which manifests as the self refers to the defiled manas, because it is constantly associated with self-delusion and the other [afflictions].
That which manifests as cognition refers to...
This refers to the other six consciousnesses,
because their apprehension of characteristics is coarse.
(Treatise)
Regarding the phrase "therefore, one is born in another stage," etc.:

Question—What is the meaning of this proof? Answer—There are two interpretations. First, it is said that the proof demonstrates that one's own [consciousness] transforms the *sahabhū-rūpa* (coexistent matter) and the *upādāya-rūpa* (derived matter) of others. Second, it is said that the proof demonstrates that one's own [consciousness] does not transform the sense organs (*indriya*) of others.
This is because both the Master [Sthiramati] and Dharmapāla agree that this does not depend on verbal expression.
The intended meaning of the proof is as follows:
if [the mind] itself can transform the support of others and their sense faculties...
Because those [objects] exist in conjunction with the bases of the sense organs of others,
they are both transformed [as objects];
since they exist solely in dependence [on those bases], when the sense organs perish, they cease to exist.
This serves as proof that at other times, [the faculties] likewise transform their basis. If this is so, why are only rebirth in another realm and entry into nirvana mentioned?
Is it not the case that other instances of death and so forth still possess the faculties? Answer: In principle, there are no faculties in those other cases.
To speak explicitly for now:
if one were born in their own realm, others might fear that this is merely a transformation of their own consciousness;
therefore, the previous explanation is correct. Question: What is the locus of dependence? [The opponent] objects.
The logical ground for its own causality would not be established;
furthermore, since that which undergoes transformation exists until the end of the kalpa, the transformed remains should likewise revert [to their original state].
Answer: It is as when one speaks of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra), where it is admitted that objects have degrees of proximity [to consciousness].
When the remains await transformation, what loss could there be for oneself or others?
The power of conditioned phenomena varies in duration;
since their transformations differ, there is no fault in their passing away.
Commentary:

Regarding the question, "What is the difference between relying on the power of consciousness and the powers of meditative concentration and supernormal knowledge? The answer is: while the body remains in a higher realm, one does not arise from the lower state through the powers of meditative concentration and supernormal knowledge.

Therefore, as explained in the commentary, there is a distinction because it gives rise to a lower, distracted consciousness (*vikṣipta-vijñāna*). Question: When giving rise to a lower, distracted consciousness, does it not rely upon a higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) through the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*)?
If this is admitted, would it not then be subsumed under meditative absorption and supernormal knowledge?

Why, then, is it separately established? Answer: It is not so; that is why it is separately established. Question: If the higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and supernormal powers (abhijñā) also serve as conditions for induction, would they not [likewise] be obtained? Answer: Even if they were induced by the meditative absorptions and supernormal powers, they belong to other stages (bhūmi).
Based on this, there is a further separate consideration. Regarding the commentary [on the phrase]:
"The body being on a lower stage, [one possesses] the divine eye, ear, and so forth."
Question: Since the divine faculties of the eye and ear occupy the same location as the matured (vipāka) eyes and ears, do they likewise perceive objects?
If they do perceive them in the same way, how is it that the matured [faculties] can perceive at a distance?
Furthermore, how can the supernormal powers of the eye and ear be manifested?
If they were not manifested, how could they perceive together?
If they did not perceive together, the two faculties would occupy the same location.
How can there be grasping and non-grasping? The answer is given by two explanations.
First, it is said that they are identical in their grasping;
what fault is there in the power of supernormal faculties inducing birth and grasping from afar?
Just as the faculties (*indriya*) of the desire realm—such as those that are nurtured (*puṣṭa*) and so forth—are alike in giving rise to consciousness, this case should be understood in the same way.
Second, they do not differ in their grasping;
the statement regarding the power of concentration and so forth refers to consciousness taking an object as its condition.
Furthermore, if the maturation of karma were capable of producing those supernormal powers,
why would it be necessary to give rise to the divine eyes and ears?
Moreover, they occupy the same location, yet their karmic forces are distinct.
The visual consciousnesses and so forth are each distinct.
What fault is there in their arising separately even at the same location?
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom):
The cultivated divine eye surpasses the physical eye;
it guides that physical eye so that it, too, can see from afar.
Commentary.
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha’s majestic light, etc.":
Question: Since Brahmā is also able to see those below by means of light, why is this not mentioned?
Answer: It is not mentioned because Brahmā can perceive what is below through his own power.
If one were to observe the eighteen thousand worlds from the side,
it would likewise be due to the Buddha’s power, as one's own power does not reach them;
furthermore, since this account is based on the upper and lower realms, it does not mention the Brahma heavens.
Commentary:

Regarding the passage stating that "the eighth [consciousness] transforms into the internal body," although it says that the eighth consciousness can transform everything by means of its power of meditative concentration and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-abhijñā*), [it does so only under specific conditions].
Regarding the passage in the commentary: "In meditative concentration, one does not perceive changes within the body;
furthermore, it is not the body itself because it lacks sense faculties."

Question: Since there is no such faculty (indriya), how can it be said that one listens to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddha? Answer: The sixth consciousness listens without depending on a faculty.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to inference (*anumāna*)."
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "from the eighth stage onward, the universal concentration is without difference," this refers to the universal wisdom (*samantajñāna*).
The concentrations are indeed distinct in their essential nature,
yet they are not different with respect to their fundamental character.
Their arising has no before or after;
their activities are similar, as stated from one perspective.
Commentary.
From this, it is known that even regarding the most distant object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
for example, when one in a lower realm gives rise to the divine eye or ear to take as objects forms in a higher realm,
the eighth consciousness of the lower realm does not take the higher realm as its object.
That is to say, the divine eye and ear do not take the eighth stage as their supporting object-substance.

Therefore, they lack a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). Question: When the distracted eyes of a higher stage see the three calamities of a lower stage, does the eighth stage of that higher realm also take those calamities as its object? Answer: In reality, it does not take them as its object.

The Protector of the Dharma (Dharmapāla) does not allow for the eighth consciousness to transform into the receptacle world of another realm. If that is so, how is the fault of the upper [realms] lacking a remote object-condition (*asamprayukta-ālambana*) to be avoided? Answer: There is no fault even if that which is transformed by the eighth consciousness of a lower realm serves as its object-condition. Question: Can the eighth consciousness, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), take the bodies and receptacle worlds of other realms as its objects? Answer: The Commentary does not provide a definitive judgment on this point.
The *Shuyao* (Essentials) and the *Dengyi* (Meaning of the Lamp) also accept this interpretation.
One commentary states: "If one transforms one's own body, it is possible [to perceive objects] of other stages, because those of lower stages can produce the divine eye and ear."
How can the power of meditative concentration transform other lands, other bodies, and the receptacle world of other lands?
And what is the purpose of such transformation?

Because the coarse and the subtle are vastly separated and do not serve as a basis for one another. If that is so, how can it be said that the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth is not determinate? This also involves no contradiction;
for the internal body and the external vessel-world transformed by the power of karma are necessarily of the same level (*bhūmi*).
If the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) transforms one’s own internal body, it is not necessarily fixed,
because a lower level can induce the divine eyes and ears of a higher level. However,
the transformation of the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*) and the bodies of others is invariably fixed.
Regarding the statement that "the transformation of the body and the receptacle world is not fixed," etc., the words are general while the intended meaning is specific;
it does not mean that both the body and the receptacle world are entirely indeterminate.

The commentary states that when one from the upper realms manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to descend to the lower realms so that those below may see them, this is called "supernatural power based on causes" because it relies upon the supernatural powers of others.
This is certainly not the case;

for when one comes from the upper realms to the lower to manifest a transformation-body (*nirmāṇa*) in the desire realm, that which is seen by those below belongs to their own level. A detailed explanation states:
If Bodhisattvas and others transform themselves into fish, earth, gold from the ocean, or curd,
do sentient beings of the lower realms receive these?
If they do not receive them, what benefit is there in such transformations?
If you grant that it is used [as an object], then how is it that the eighth consciousness of a sentient being does not take that as its object?
If it does not take it as an object, then the experience would not be "consciousness-only.
Therefore, one knows that through the supernatural power of another, the transformation of the bodies, receptacles, and environments of other stages is induced.
That which supports the dust-particles is what is called the "body.

Since fish, gold, curd, and so forth do not belong to the desire realm, if one were to offer this defense: that the six consciousnesses of sentient beings rely upon rice and other such things transformed by Bodhisattvas and others.
To claim that the underlying substance (*bhāva*) transforms and then functions as the object is also untenable—
just as in the case where the eye-consciousness takes the lower three realms as its conditions and relies upon the transformation of the eighth consciousness in the lower realm as its substance.
This too is incorrect.
Even if one grants that [the objects] are transformations of the six [consciousnesses] themselves,
what harm is there in saying that the eighth consciousness arises from its own fundamental state through supernatural power?
For it is not the same as the objects of ordinary times.
It was stated previously that the upper eye relies upon the eighth [consciousness] below;
however, because the upper eighth [consciousness] cannot take what is below as its object,
this is so for the following reason:
If those in the higher [realms] were to transform the lower calamities themselves,
they would be useless there because of the vast disparity between the coarse and the subtle. Therefore,
they must take the calamities transformed by those in the lower eight [realms] as their objective basis before they can transform them.
What purpose would transformation serve?
Furthermore, because it is not induced by supernormal powers (abhijñā), it does not undergo transformation.
If it were transformed into fish or rice, it would therefore be useful.
Furthermore, by what means could supernormal powers (abhijñā) be cited as an analogous case?
If you do not allow for transformation because of the distinction between the coarse and the subtle,
then it would follow that the other six consciousnesses should likewise not take [the object] as their condition.

Because the coarse and the subtle are separated; if that were so, it would result in the fault of [the mind] lacking the eight conditions for the outflow-free state. Answer: There is no contradiction, because there is no direct apprehension (*pratyakṣa*).
If one says that transformation occurs only through direct application, [then the fault remains].
The eighth [transformation] should not transform the sensory dusts (viṣaya) that support others;
nor should the sixth [consciousness] transform the bodies of bodhisattvas, fish, and so forth,
because these are not objects of direct personal use.

If one were to grant that [the object] is used directly, it would no longer be "mere consciousness" (vijñaptimātra). Furthermore, the treatise explicitly states that [the object] is determined by the power of meditative concentration, the realm, the stage, and whether it belongs to oneself or another; yet you do not accept this as definitive.
Why then do you insist on such arbitrary distinctions that lead to so many contradictions?
It may be said that one can rest at ease while with a snake; furthermore, it is also illogical to claim that when [a being] comes up to manifest a transformation in the desire realm,
they see their own level from below.
It is said that they manifest as transformations because they resemble the desire realm; in reality, however,
they are bound to the higher stages.
The dharmas of the desire realm cannot be acquired through cultivation or transformed;
this will be explained in detail below.
Commentary.
Regarding "attaining the concentration of majestic power" (*vaśitā-samādhi*):
the superior concentration produced by those who possess majestic power is called the concentration of majestic power.
There are two interpretations of this: first, it refers to the concentration attained by sovereign Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"It is not the case that all concentrated minds possess the capacity to produce this form;
rather, only a specific class [of them] possesses it."
Therefore, it is known that [this state] belongs only to the noble ones (*ārya*).
A second interpretation holds that it also extends to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), provided they have long practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and attained mastery (*vaśitā*).
This excludes those who lack such mastery, designating them as "those belonging to a single class" (*ekajātīya*).
There is no fault in this either;
the previous interpretation is superior.
(Commentary)
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that the eyes, ears, and so forth belong to the first dhyāna:
this is out of order.

It should properly have been placed earlier, following the statement concerning the objects of the divine eye and ear. Question: Previously, it was clarified whether the essential nature of the eye and ear exists or not.
With what intention does he next state that the eye and ear have the same and different objects of connection with the higher realms? Answer:
Although the substance was previously clarified, the distinctions regarding their mutual connection had not yet been discussed; therefore, they are explained next.
Although the substance (*dravya*) and the appearance (*nimitta*) differ, because they both constitute the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), it is said:

"Furthermore, [it is] explained. Question: Do the eyes and so forth of the first dhyāna possess a substantial basis (*mūla-dravya*) when seeing the forms of higher stages? Answer: Although this is not explicitly stated, by principle it must exist.
Taking that which is transformed by another eighth consciousness as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*).
Commentary:
Because of this, the objects known by these three consciousnesses must necessarily be identical.
Since the objective-image portions (*nimittabhāga*) of the three consciousnesses— eye, ear, and body— belong exclusively to the first dhyāna,
the objective-images of the eye and ear do not belong to the higher realms.
(Commentary)

Regarding the fifty-fourth point, "due to the deficiency of the cause for arising," there are briefly two interpretations of the meaning of "deficiency of the cause": First, it is said that "cause" refers to the seed;
since those [beings] lack seeds, it is called a "deficiency of the cause. Second, it is said that "cause" carries the sense of "the reason why" (the underlying condition).

Because of the principle that those [objects], such as fragrance, are non-arisen. Question: Even if one were to grant their existence, what principle would it contradict? Answer: If one grants that fragrance and taste manifest to a concentrated mind (samāhita-citta).
If fragrance and taste were bound to the higher stages according to the mind,
then fragrance and taste would exist in those higher stages;
this would contradict the fault of various scriptural teachings.
Based on this, the concentrated mind does not change with respect to odor or flavor;
combined with the explanations provided in the *Śāstra*, these form three interpretations.
It is stated that the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) is precisely the cause.
Alternatively, the explanation provided by the *Vyākhyā* does not differ from the previous two;
it states that the cause of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) is precisely those two preceding ones.
There is nothing else besides this.
[The] Commentary [states]:
"Furthermore, it is useless."
Fragrance and flavor are established based upon edible food;
since they have no edible food,
what would fragrance and flavor be for, even if they were present?
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "either the fundamental [consciousness] and its transformations," the names assigned to them respectively refer to those that necessarily pervade both form and mind.
Because they all arise based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are collectively termed "fruits" (*phala*). [The] Commentary [states]:
"All are both transformative (*nairmāṇika*) and emanated (*nirmāṇa*)."
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) refers to the alteration and change of a substance;
manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) refers to the sudden appearance of what was previously non-existent.
The Buddha is capable of performing both through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "penetration can induce the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)," etc.:

Question: If, when one is in the two states of a Buddha, mental factors are always associated, how can there be distinctions between the faculties, objects, and the induced meditative concentration? Answer: Although they arise simultaneously, [there are distinctions].
Because their functional power differs, there is a distinction in what they transform;
yet, what exactly is it that is transformed?
Furthermore, an untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) must necessarily arise simultaneously with meditative concentration and the Path.
The single volition associated [with these states] is termed "concentration" and "path-precept" (mārga-śīla) in relation to these two,
because the two assist the volition by providing restraint and prevention.
Now, although concentration and [the path-precept] both apply to both [types of restraint] and occur simultaneously, [they are distinguished by their respective functions].

The two—the produced matter (*rūpa*) and so forth, and the producer—are termed "fixed" (*niyata*). What fault would there be in this being common to both [the meditative concentration] and the precepts?
The Commentary states:
"By the power of concentration, the body and the environment are transformed."
Although the meaning was briefly explained previously to clarify the penetration [of the faculties],
no scriptural evidence was yet cited;
now, as I provide full citations, I bring it up again.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "transforming the body into ten billion [forms]," according to that treatise, it says:
Regarding the subtlety of the mind’s sovereign operation:
this refers to all forms within the two realms of form and formlessness.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "There are devas who possess equanimous minds."
Having previously, among human beings, thus and thus refined, polished,
and clarified their minds through such cultivation, they abide within a space the size of a single hair-tip,
moving back and forth in succession without obstructing one another. Commentary:
The two kinds of form in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are called "mastery" (vaśitā):
first, that which manifests through a concentrated mind;
second, the form resulting from the retribution induced by mastery-concentration (vaśitā-samādhi).
In the formless realm, there is only that which is manifested by a single,
fixed state of mind. Because the form of the two meditative absorptions arises through mastery over meditative concentration,
it is called the subtle nature of mental mastery.
The cited sūtra, as explained in the commentaries, merely serves to prove that the retributive form (*vipākaja-rūpa*) of the form realm consists of the so-called "pure abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*),
such as the gods of Equal Mind (*samjñisattva*). It describes how these beings,
with bodies sixteen thousand *yojanas* in height, approach the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.
Each one dwells upon a patch of ground the size of a hair-tip, just as the light of lamps does not obstruct one another.
Furthermore, those Bodhisattvas of the ten stages above the Śuddhāvāsa heavens are called the Devas of Equal Mind (*Samacitta*). Detailed explanation follows:
If one can also arise from the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and come to the Buddha’s presence, they are called "gods of equal mind" (*samacittadeva*).
What fault is there in this?
For the sutra does not make such a distinction.
Furthermore, the treatise speaks of both [realms] above;
why then does the cited proof establish only the Form Realm?
Therefore, it is known that there is no contradiction in its establishing [the principle] generally.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* does not state that they were established in common;
perhaps they were originally different,
or perhaps the commentator, relying on other texts, stated that they were established in common.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 93, states:
"Sixty gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven sit upon the tip of a single needle.
Furthermore, those in the realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and formlessness (*arūpya-dhātu*) do not obstruct one another, each according to their own kind."
It is not that these two realms do not obstruct one another.
At first glance, that passage appears to state that the two realms do not obstruct one another.
[Commentary:]
Regarding the statement that the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is also said to have beings who cause one another to see:
since the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the various devas of the Form Realm also transform their bodies and so forth,
we know this applies not only to the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
As for the fact that some copies of the *Śū* (Commentary) write it as "she" (設), etc., this is a scribal error;
"shuo" (說) is correct.
[End of] Commentary.
It should also follow that [the mind] does not take as its object those *niṣyanda-rūpa* (outflowing matter) and so forth that are interrupted.

Question: Excluding the *vipāka-rūpa* (resultant matter) produced by karma, all other things—namely, the various wholesome and unwholesome [phenomena] as well as external objects and so forth—are termed *niṣyanda*.
Is it not the case that the cause for interruption is unestablished for one part and for both together? Answer: The commentary briefly indicates the principle;
a full exposition should be concise.
Once the principle is distinguished, it can be understood.
Furthermore, the intent of the commentary is to demonstrate that the preceding inference is inconclusive;
it does not constitute a refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus says the treatise.
Briefly explaining this consciousness up to the manifested transformed matter (*rūpa*):
Question— Since the eighth [consciousness] takes real matter within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as its object,
do the five [sensory consciousnesses] also take it as their object?
If they were not objects of cognition, then while noble ones might transform fish and other such things, ordinary beings should not perceive them.
If one grants that they are objects of cognition, then the visible forms included within the fifty-four sites of teaching would be non-visible and non-obstructive.
Furthermore, how is this reconciled? The answer is as previously analyzed regarding the second lamp.
Another interpretation states that it transforms the matter of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rūpa*) such that it lacks visibility and resistance (*sapratigha*).
"However, it is called 'seeing gold' and so forth because it serves as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the eye and other faculties.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "In this context, there is an objection which should be considered according to reason":
Objection:
Since causes follow their effects, they are subsumed within the dharma-dhātu;

since objects correspond to the mind, they are subsumed within the consciousness-dhātu. Answer: Because causes and conditions directly manifest the essence [of the effect], [the cause is subsumed under the dharma-dhātu].
The seeds are subsumed under the present [moment], because they induce other [seeds] as distant objects; therefore, they are not included within the locus of the dharma (*dharmāyatana*).
— Commentary.
Regarding "extremely condensed" (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*) and "extremely remote" (*paramāṇu-vivikta*) matter:
that which is reduced from roots, vessels, and so forth down to atoms is called "extremely condensed";
that which is reduced from reflected images and so forth down to atoms is called "extremely remote."
Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "if it is only the mental faculty that conditions," this refers to the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which arises through discrimination by taking the sense faculties and their objects as its conditions.
It is also called "comprised within that which arises from pervasive conceptualization.
In the Commentary:
"To follow the light by means of darkness" means...
That which is hidden and obscured is called "darkness," while that which is manifest and revealed is called "light.
Regarding the ten bases (*āyatana*), the meaning of designating the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) as either light or darkness can now be definitively established.
[Commentary].
Regarding the phrase "nor is it because [the sixth consciousness] reaches [its object], nor because it takes existence as its condition":

the intended meaning is that although the sixth [consciousness] shares the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses] and is termed "discriminative," it possesses the functional capacity to engage with its objects.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the former must necessarily have a function and the latter must necessarily have an object," the sub-commentary explains the two transformations of causes and conditions through four interpretations in total.
One may understand this by examining the fourth explanation. According to one interpretation, there are three explanations:

first, it is said that only the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is called "transformation due to causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*), whereas all forms of inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*abhūta-pramāṇa*) are "conceptual transformation" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*).
The second [master] says that the eighth consciousness-king is called "transformation through causal conditions" (*nidāna-pariṇāma*),
while the remaining minds and mental factors are called "transformation through discrimination" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*).
The third says that only the eighth mind-king is "transformation through causal conditions."
The associated mental factors (*caitta*) also undergo transformation through differentiation;
this is the meaning of Dharmapāla’s doctrine.
For it is only the mind-king (*cittarāja*) that maintains the seeds and receives perfuming (*vāsanā*).
He himself judges that the first two [positions] involve many faults, while the third can be reconciled.

Question: If it is said that the objects of the eye and other faculties, such as visible forms, have no ultimate utility, then do the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth all take only conventional (prajñapti) dharmas as their objects?

Answer: Although there are names for the conventional, they exist based on their own meanings; since the conventional is taught in dependence upon the real, it is not an object of the five sensory consciousnesses.
This is the mind of conceptual discrimination.
Because its meaning is explained separately,
although reflected images, forms, and so forth are unimpeded, they are designated as "provisional form."
However, it is said that what arises from seeds is itself called the "real";
therefore, there is no fault. To explain in detail:
not only do the former two [positions] have many faults.
Thus, the third interpretation is also subject to the same fault as before. Why is this?
Because, for example, the eighth consciousness arises spontaneously.
The objects transformed [by consciousness] that arise from actual seeds are termed "transformation by causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*).

These include a portion of the five *pravṛtti-vijñānas*, as well as the sixth consciousness when it arises simultaneously with them and functions spontaneously to perceive objects; these also arise from cultivation and are produced from actual seeds.
Why, then, is it immediately judged to be a conceptual transformation?
Therefore, we now rely on the fourth fascicle of the Commentary (*Sū*).
The Commentary states:

Regarding the statement that "a single moment of mind can become two kinds [of transformation]," that which conditions the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is termed transformation through causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That which conditions the seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*) is subsumed under transformation through discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Commentary:
This is an indirect demonstration that the eight [consciousnesses] all possess both types of transformation.
The primary consciousness (the king) and the secondary consciousnesses (its objects) are, respectively, subsumed under the two transformations of causal conditions and conceptual discrimination.
Treatise:
Regarding the claim that transformed minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) and so forth cannot take [them] as objects because they are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states:
Regarding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), it has no self-reliance; its mind relies upon another.
As explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:
"That is to say, the minds of transformation and so forth manifest in dependence upon the real mind."
It is merely the aspect of the real mind that appears as if it were a mind possessing objects and mental activity;
like fire in a mirror, it has no separate self-substance. The meaning of this explanation is as follows:
The mind whose own supporting [aspect]—the real seeing-part—is absent is called "without its own support.

However, that which possesses a semblance of deliberation is called "having another as its support. Furthermore, the seeing-part, the self-verifying part, and the verifying-of-self-verifying part are called the "mind with its own support."
The transformative mind differs from those;
it is called "having no self-support but depending on another's mind," which may be understood as before.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "namely, the two means of valid cognition, direct perception and inference... up to 'should be distinguished accordingly,'" it is as follows:

for example, when the sixth consciousness (the mental faculty) takes a previously experienced real object as its condition, it perfumes and thereby produces a real seed; subsequently, this gives rise to a present realization.
Although this is subsumed under conceptual transformation through inference (*anumāna-vikalpa-vikṛti*),
it may possess practical efficacy;
likewise, the sixth [consciousness], direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which shares the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses], also possesses practical efficacy.
If the concentrated mind takes the eighteen realms as its object, one should understand—
as previously explained— that it functions by encompassing both the provisional and the real.
(Commentary)
In this context, "small" refers to the body-vessel (*deha-bhājana*);
here, the body itself is the vessel,
not the external vessel-world (*bāhya-bhājana*).
Regarding the fifty-one [mental factors], the distinction between broad and narrow is clarified based on the body and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
Some commentaries explain this by taking both the body and the vessel-world as the basis;
however, we do not follow this approach here.
That treatise merely explains "narrow" and "vast" based on the objects of appropriation (*upātta*).
A detailed examination reveals that it fails to grasp the essential meaning of the *Śāstra* and is thus rendered utterly trivial.
Please examine this carefully.
